blurb: Who builds AI, open versus closed models, the DeepSeek shock, and how the money works.

cards.title: Two ways to release a model

steps.p: The company keeps the model on its own servers. You use it through an app or API but never get the model itself — like ChatGPT or Claude.
The company publishes the trained parameters for anyone to download and run — like Meta's Llama or DeepSeek's models.
Truly open-source software lets you see how it was built. Most "open" models share the finished parameters but not the training data or full recipe.
steps.analogy: Being given a cake, versus being given the recipe and ingredients list too.

steps.p: Businesses can run open models privately on their own servers, customise them and avoid depending on one supplier.
The best open models have usually trailed the best closed ones by about a year or less — sometimes much less.

options: Open source also shares enough about training data and code to rebuild the model
Open source is always free and open-weight costs money
cards.why: The recipe. Open weights give you the finished model. Open source, by the usual definition, also lets you see and reproduce how it was made.

cards.statement: Meta's Llama models count as open source under the Open Source Initiative's definition.
cards.why: False. Llama's licence has usage restrictions and the training data isn't released, so it's open-weight, not open source by that standard.

cards.q: A main reason a company might pick an open-weight model is to…
options: Run it privately on its own servers and customise it
Get it to answer faster than any closed model
cards.why: Control and privacy. Sensitive data never leaves the company, and it can fine-tune the model however it likes.

cards.title: Meta's first LLaMA model leaked onto the internet within about a week of its limited release in 2023.
cards.detail: Meta had shared it only with approved researchers. The leak sparked a wave of open experimentation — and Meta released later versions openly by choice.

cards.statement: The best open-weight models have generally trailed the best closed models by around a year or less.
cards.why: True. Analyses like Epoch AI's put the gap at roughly a year, and it narrowed sharply when DeepSeek-R1 arrived.

steps.p: OpenAI (ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google DeepMind (Gemini), Meta (Llama) and xAI (Grok) lead, backed by enormous computing budgets.
Many labs share roots: Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI researchers; Google merged its two AI groups into Google DeepMind.
DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot and others release strong models, often open-weight, despite limits on buying top US chips.
France's Mistral AI is Europe's best-known model maker. Many others focus on applications rather than the largest models.
Cloud giants pair with labs: Microsoft with OpenAI; Amazon and Google with Anthropic. Labs get computing, clouds get customers.
steps.analogy: Like car makers teaming up with engine makers.

options: Former OpenAI researchers, including Dario and Daniela Amodei
cards.why: Ex-OpenAI researchers. A group left to start a company with a stronger focus on AI safety.

cards.statement: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a nonprofit.
cards.why: True. It later added a capped-profit company to raise the huge sums needed for computing.

cards.q: In 2023, Google merged two AI groups to form Google DeepMind. They were…
cards.why: Brain and DeepMind. Two rival in-house teams combined to compete with OpenAI.

cards.title: DeepSeek is funded by High-Flyer, a Chinese hedge fund that uses computer-driven trading.
cards.detail: The fund had stockpiled GPUs for trading research. Founder Liang Wenfeng spun out DeepSeek in 2023 to pursue general AI.

cards.statement: Mistral AI is based in France.
cards.why: True. Founded in Paris in 2023 by former Google DeepMind and Meta researchers.

steps.p: Chinese lab DeepSeek released R1, a reasoning model rivalling OpenAI's best, free to download.
DeepSeek reported about $5.6 million of computing for the final training run of the model it was built on — tiny next to rivals' rumoured budgets.

steps.h: But that's not the full bill
steps.p: The figure excluded research, failed experiments, staff and the chips themselves — likely hundreds of millions overall.
steps.analogy: Quoting the cost of the final exam, not the years of school before it.

steps.p: Investors wondered if AI would need far fewer chips. NVIDIA's market value fell by about $600 billion in one day.
The Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper, people often use so much more of it that total demand rises.

cards.statement: DeepSeek's ~$5.6 million figure covered the full cost of developing the model.
cards.hint: The final exam, not the schooling.
cards.why: False. It covered the computing for the final training run only — not research, earlier experiments, staff or buying the hardware.

cards.q: Why did cheap-training claims rattle chip stocks?
options: They suggested AI might need far less spending on GPUs than expected
cards.why: Fear of lower demand. If great models need far fewer chips, the boom in chip sales might slow.

cards.q: The Jevons paradox suggests that making AI cheaper to run might…
options: Increase total demand, as cheaper AI gets used far more
Make chips more expensive to build
cards.why: More total use. Cheaper steam engines led to more coal burned, not less. Cheaper AI may similarly mean more chips.

cards.title: DeepSeek released R1 under the permissive MIT licence.
cards.detail: That let anyone use, change and sell products built on it with almost no restrictions, and it quickly appeared on major cloud platforms.

cards.statement: DeepSeek's app briefly became the top free app on Apple's US App Store.
cards.why: True. In late January 2025 it briefly overtook ChatGPT there, as curiosity about the cheap, strong model spread.

steps.p: Labs spend billions on chips, data centers, electricity and researchers. Training is expensive, and serving millions of users daily is too.
Subscriptions (like $20-a-month plans), businesses paying per token through the API, and enterprise deals.
The cost of getting GPT-4-level performance has fallen by orders of magnitude since 2023, thanks to better models and hardware.

visual.caption: Illustration: roughly 10× cheaper each year for the same ability.

steps.p: ChatGPT reached an estimated 100 million users about two months after launch — faster than any app before it.
Can revenue grow fast enough to justify hundreds of billions in spending? Investors are betting yes; sceptics warn of a bubble.

cards.q: How has the price of reaching GPT-4-level performance changed since 2023?
cards.why: Down 10× or more, repeatedly. Smaller, better-trained models and cheaper hardware keep driving the price down.

cards.statement: ChatGPT reached an estimated 100 million users about two months after launch.
cards.why: True. Analyst estimates put it at about two months — then the fastest-growing consumer app ever recorded.

cards.q: Which two cloud giants made major investments in Anthropic?
cards.why: Amazon and Google. Each invested billions, and Anthropic uses their cloud computing to train and serve Claude.

cards.title: ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022 as a "low-key research preview".
cards.detail: OpenAI staff reportedly expected modest interest. It reached a million users in five days and set off the generative AI boom.

cards.title: Read the source, not the headline
cards.body: AI news often exaggerates — "$5 million model" or "AI replaces X". The original report usually has important caveats.
cards.challenge: Pick one AI headline this week and find the original paper or announcement. Note one thing the headline left out.
